items.summary: Unrefereed research candidate. In one sentence: the matrix geometric mean can jump at singular matrices, every possible jump is described by one rank condition, and the same mechanism refutes a published claim that the symbol of the geometric mean of two GLT matrix-sequences is always the geometric mean of their symbols. The geometric mean A#B of two positive definite matrices is the matrix analogue of √(ab), used to average covariance matrices and structured matrices and to define the Matsumoto fidelity of quantum states. It need not be continuous at singular pairs. Theorem 1 shows that X is a limit of A j #B j with positive definite A j → A, B j → B exactly when X ≽ 0, the block matrix [[A, X], [X, B]] is positive semidefinite and its rank is at most the dimension N (a dilation description with an auxiliary contraction already follows from recent work of Jones; the explicit elimination is the contribution). At equal inputs this gives the full set of limits and the exact interval of limiting Matsumoto fidelities. For generalized locally Toeplitz (GLT) matrix-sequences, uniformly bounded positive definite inputs with identical scalar symbols can have geometric means with the wrong symbol (4/5 instead of 1 on half the interval) or no eigenvalue distribution at all. This refutes Theorem 4 and Conjecture 1 of the arXiv version of Ilyas, Khan, Loi and Serra-Capizzano and, according to an AI-assisted reading of the published text, Theorem 3 and Conjecture 1 of their article in Linear Algebra Appl. (2025); the failing step of the proof is located. Positive results: closure for every Kubo-Ando mean when the sum of the symbols is positive definite almost everywhere; a one-sided theorem that the regularised symbol is always an upper envelope; and, for bounded Riemann-integrable scalar symbols of the space variable only, a sharp dichotomy (the formula holds for every realisation if and only if the symbols have no common zero set of positive measure or essentially disjoint supports). The classical two-dimensional discontinuity, Ando's maximal characterisation and the envelope X ≼ A#B are earlier work and are credited. The archive contains the manuscript (PDF and Markdown source), two figures with the script that draws them, an exact verifier (verify_exact.py, Python standard library only, 1,030 rational and Gaussian-rational checks of closed forms and finite assemblies, with a mutation self-test) and its retained output, the bibliography with its Crossref/arXiv records, the dated novelty ledger, a revision note, CI and SHA-256 sums. Assurance: written proofs; the verifier checks finite exact identities, not the theorems' limits or quantifiers; internal AI-assisted review only (not human peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification). items.summary: Automated sleep staging supports summary sleep measures, but the best use of a limited review budget remains uncertain. We present two development analyses of simulated review against expert sleep-stage references. In BOAS, training-derived quantities from 40 participants were compared across review policies in 20 previously inspected participants, using existing PSG and wearable headband predictions. At a 10% budget, mean absolute error in sleep time restricted to reference-scorable epochs was 7.725 minutes without review, 6.951 with random review, 4.475 with sleep-wake disagreement, and 6.250 with a conditional-risk rule. A reference-mask-conditioned bias correction yielded 11.888 minutes and is not a deployable automatic baseline. A separate Sleep-EDF feasibility probe used the same YASA model on two EEG leads from six selected participants; five were scored after one HTTP failure. Corresponding mean errors were 107.6 minutes without review, 95.7 with random review, 87.3 with model entropy, and 77.2 with lead disagreement. The BOAS source model's participant-level out-of-fold status and Sleep-EDF pretraining overlap are unverified; the latter also raised an unresolved scikit-learn version warning. The analyses use different inputs, selection rules and recording durations, and neither is independent validation. Perfect reference substitution was simulated, conditional outcomes are not full-night clinical total sleep time, and no human review time was measured. These exploratory findings do not establish clinical utility or generalizable superiority.
items.title: Allocating a Simulated Review Budget to Sleep–Wake Disagreements: Exploratory Analyses of Two Public Datasets

items.summary: Abstract: Classical inferential statistics and p-value hypothesis testing in healthcare big data repositories suffer from severe structural limitations, notably p-hacking, asymptotic N-bias, and the frequent violation of independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) assumptions due to intra-patient longitudinal dependencies, hospital clustering, and epidemiological shockwaves. To overcome these failures, we introduce an Inverse Breakpoint Analysis, a scale-invariant, physics-inspired metrological audit framework. Our analysis treats discrete clinical event counts not as abstract probabilities, but as physical informational mass. Grounded in Garwood exact discrete limits and Wilson-Hilferty approximations, the framework extends our previous work on stress testing indices for Big health data and establishes three rigorous thresholds: a pure mass saturation limit, a baseline tolerance band, and a structural signal threshold. Through the use of these three parameters, our inverse breakpoint analysis eliminates false-positive artifacts induced by massive repository sizes while preventing under-powering in small cohorts. Ultimately, the framework demonstrates that percentage-based thresholds are kinematic artifacts of scale, whereas absolute excess discrete mass serves as the sole physical invariant for healthcare data validation. We validated this approach with numerous illustrative examples.
items.title: Inverse Breakpoint Analysis: A Scale-Invariant Physics-Inspired Metrological Audit for Sanitary Big Data

items.summary: Memory systems for LLM agents are evaluated mostly on social dialogue, where facts accumulate and rarely change, so remembering reduces largely to finding the turn in which something was said. Financial dialogue breaks this assumption: figures are revised, stances shift without being restated, rules stated once govern later questions, and a single company is discussed under several analytical lenses. Memory systems that retrieve the passages most similar to a question, or the most recent ones, therefore return superseded values, miss rules that share no wording with the question, and cannot recover a stance spread across sessions. We present TrackMem, a per-speaker graph memory that tracks the history of figures, separates perspectives by entity and lens, and preserves each speaker's actions in chronological order. To evaluate it, we introduce FinLoCoMo, a benchmark of 15 long-horizon investment conversations with 765 questions in two splits: one following the LoCoMo categories and one targeting four failure modes. With two readers, TrackMem outperforms existing memory systems on both splits. On the failure-mode split it reaches 73.9% macro accuracy against 69.4% for the strongest baseline, with the largest gains on questions about revised figures (86.5% against 73.4%).
items.title: TrackMem: Tracking Evolving Beliefs in Long-Horizon Financial Dialogue

items.summary: Although self-improvement is becoming increasingly important as tasks become more complex, models struggle to generate reliable supervision for harder, out-of-distribution instances. One way to address this challenge is to exploit compositional structure: models often solve simpler subproblems more reliably than full problems, so their subproblem predictions can be composed into supervision for harder ones. We systematically study when this kind of composed supervision supports self-improvement and when it fails. Our controlled experiments identify three failure modes: unreliable subproblem predictions, errors introduced by composition, and limited supervision coverage. Beyond controlled settings, these findings carry over to more realistic coding and reasoning tasks: composed labels are more accurate than direct self-generated labels and improve performance even on compositions longer than those seen during training, while the failure modes remain visible. Further, although these failure modes often keep compositional self-improvement from fully succeeding on its own, a short SFT warmup with compositional self-improvement can bootstrap reinforcement learning on tasks that require composing skills the model already has, particularly when direct exploration rarely succeeds. Together, these findings characterize when compositional self-improvement can provide sufficiently reliable supervision to expand model capabilities.
items.title: Compositional Self-Improvement: Promises and Pitfalls

items.summary: Reliable forensic evidence extraction from mobile SQLite databases is challenging because application schemas are undocumented, evolve across releases, and differ across operating systems, making schema-specific methods brittle and difficult to maintain. We present SNEEF, a symbolic-neural framework for context-aware evidence extraction that encodes each SQLite row as context-value pairs with standardized provenance metadata and column labels, uses a language model to recognize nine forensic entity types, and binds each accepted entity to its source table and row through the PA-EEP provenance protocol. We evaluate SNEEF against examiner-verified ground truth from five corpora built from public Android and iOS device images, spanning multiple application versions. SNEEF achieves an F1 score of 0.967 for evidence entities extracted from SQLite row content, excluding application names, compared with 0.728 for a context-free configuration, with consistent gains across all corpora. We also introduce an Evidence Failure Mode taxonomy to characterize why extraction errors occur.
items.title: A Symbolic-Neural Framework for Context-Aware Evidence Extraction from Mobile SQLite Databases

items.summary: There are many causal discovery algorithms, but few guiding principles for choosing between them. Methods are usually compared through three lenses: identifiability, consistency, and benchmarks. Each introduces assumptions about the data-generating process that are often untestable. We argue that there are no shared standards for comparing, prioritizing, or even discussing those assumptions. We support this claim by showing that (i) identifiability assumptions are often preferred by convention rather than by principle, (ii) uniform consistency requires further untestable assumptions, while the weaker pointwise consistency has arguably narrowed algorithm design, and (iii) benchmarks are not neutral tests but carry an epistemic role of their own: they quietly fix which regimes matter, which guarantees come into play, and what counts as success. In doing so, they shape what algorithm comparisons are taken to show and thus perform some of the same epistemic work as theory, but less transparently. In this position paper we argue for a more transparent, integrated practice: Make the epistemic standards for discussing identifiability and consistency assumptions explicit, especially their failure modes and scope conditions; design benchmarks to operationalize those standards, by stress-testing and ablating both. Then, theoretical and empirical results jointly clarify when, why, and how algorithms may work rather than accumulate as disconnected advances.
items.title: Causal discovery needs explicit epistemic standards

items.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training improves the single-sample quality of visual generative models, but deployment often provides additional inference compute through Best-of-N sampling. Whether RL gains transfer under such test-time scaling, particularly on difficult held-out tasks, remains poorly understood in the visual domain. Our central contribution is to systematically identify and characterize a failure mode of scaling transfer in visual RL: across multiple RL methods, model backbones, and evaluations spanning compositional generation, text rendering, and preference alignment, higher single-sample reward does not necessarily imply a better quality-compute frontier. RL gains may attenuate, saturate, or even reverse at large sampling budgets, with the base model eventually outperforming its post-trained counterpart. We explain these regimes through a quantile-transfer framework, showing that Best-of-N places increasing weight on the upper tail of the reward distribution as N grows. Consequently, RL can improve typical samples while compressing or degrading the rare high-quality outcomes that test-time scaling exploits. As a simple intervention motivated by this analysis, we introduce Quantile Utility Policy Optimization (QUPO), which optimizes a controllable mixture of quantile utilities corresponding to different inference budgets. Experiments on SD3.5-M and BAGEL show that QUPO better preserves upper-tail quality and substantially improves scaling on challenging held-out prompts relative to standard RL post-training. Our results suggest that visual generative models should be evaluated and optimized not only for single-sample quality, but for how post-training reshapes the full reward distribution that inference-time scaling exploits.
items.title: Do Visual RL Gains Scale at Test Time? A Quantile View of Post-Training

items.summary: Indirect prompt injection creates a distinctive risk for blue-team Large Language Model (LLM) agents in Security Operations Centers (SOCs). Malicious instructions can be embedded in telemetry, tickets, retrieval results, or memory and then propagate through alert triage, incident summarization, response recommendation, and Indicator of Compromise (IOC) extraction as locally plausible intermediate decisions. We characterize this failure mode as evidence-chain contamination of protected task state. The main challenge is task dependent: a suspicious string may be malicious control text for summarization but essential evidence for IOC extraction. To address this challenge, we propose StateFence, a task-aware evaluation and defense framework that treats severity labels, incident narratives, response policies, and IOC sets as protected states. StateFence maps indirect prompt-injection attacks into explicit, stealth, multi-hop, and persistent SOC evidence attacks, records observable propagation traces, and routes defenses according to the attacked state. Across controlled SOC cases and public-SOC validation cases, StateFence lowers attack success and reduces failures that appear only after evidence is poisoned, while preserving task utility and avoiding the indicator loss caused by task-mismatched filtering. Our findings indicate that robust blue-team LLM agents require mechanisms that preserve task-critical state under untrusted evidence.
items.title: StateFence: Task-State Protection Against Evidence-Chain Contamination in Blue-Team LLM Agents

items.summary: Repeated passive seismic surveys were conducted over more than a decade on the unstable La Praz rock slope in Savoie, France, which involved an estimated rock volume of approximately 13,000--15,000 m${}^3$. The final survey took place two months before the complete collapse of the slope in August 2023. The amplitude of the Horizontal-to-Vertical Spectral Ratio at the peak frequency (*aHVSR(fp)*) was used to distinguish stable and unstable areas and identify fractures associated with significant mechanical decoupling. Rock compartments were also classified according to their rockfall hazard. The compartments most susceptible to failure exhibited the highest *aHVSR(fp)* values, ranging from 26 to 157, compared with values of 7.5--19 in intermediate-hazard areas and 2.7 in the adjacent stable rock mass. The main HVSR peak frequency (*fp*) exhibited distinct decreases of 15%, 14%, and 11% in three unstable rock compartments before the collapse. These reductions substantially exceeded the range of environmentally induced resonance-frequency fluctuations observed at the site and commonly reported in the literature as a limitation of this method. The frequency decreases were interpreted as indicators of progressive damage extending into the rock slope. Notably, these changes were detected exclusively in the three compartments identified as the most susceptible to failure, which also exhibited the highest *aHVSR(fp)* values. This study demonstrates, for the first time, the potential of passive seismic monitoring to reveal progressive in-depth damage within a complex, heterogeneous, and highly fractured rock slope. The findings highlight the value of combining HVSR amplitude and peak-frequency variations to characterize unstable rock compartments and identify potential precursors to catastrophic slope failure.
items.title: Mapping rockfall hazard and detecting precursory damage in rock slopes with passive seismic: Lessons from the La Praz case-study

items.summary: We introduce Synergetic Autonomous Intelligence (SAI), a theory and design program for learning systems that form, preserve, revise, and compose relations while continuing to learn. SAI is built on three axioms: consequential distinctions must not become orphaned (U); identity is determined by future-faithful continuation under a declared contract (I); and unresolved defects are repaired by the least lawful local completion at the lowest admitted grade (L). We model a model, agent, tool, team, or environment boundary as a recursive semi-closed system with a Kernel-Ring representation, a Compile-Open-Participate cycle, and a typed residual comparing actual with claimed continuation. Under explicit finite or affine contracts, we establish relative consistency and conditional non-redundancy of U/I/L, characterize a contract-relative semantic quotient, construct an exact joint stochastic refinement, derive a constrained residual contraction, prove finite-horizon continued-service viability, and give an executed-intervention identification result with an observational-confounding boundary. We define GRC-Close as the generative and repair schema for this contract. The framework also gives finite contracts for action-effect-feedback loop re-entry, partial failure, duplicate-effect idempotency, replay, concurrent delivery, causal uncertainty, and threshold-radix state representation. KREIT, the Kernel-Ring Equilibrium Information Theory layer, treats information as a typed, resource-bounded distinction; the control layer authorizes, executes, audits, and updates actions across cloud-edge-end scales. These results establish a common contract-level vocabulary for representation, relation, memory, action, communication, explanation, coordination, and growth, while marking the assumptions and open boundaries required for later generalization.
items.title: Synergetic Autonomous Intelligence: Three Axioms for Recursive Semi-Closed Learning

items.summary: Root cause analysis (RCA) in microservice systems requires distinguishing failure sources from routine fluctuations and propagated symptoms. Small language models (SLMs) offer a practical solution under cost and privacy constraints, and recent approaches improve their capabilities through structured diagnostic procedures. However, performing diagnostic analysis does not ensure correct root-cause identification. Our empirical study shows that final decisions often favor large anomaly scores despite the model's own propagation analysis suggesting otherwise. Moreover, the input does not reveal whether these apparently anomalous signals are common during normal operation. These findings motivate our system, which improves how SLMs assess evidence and select root causes through Historical Frequency Profiling and Biased-Decision Correction. Historical Frequency Profiling quantifies how often metric and log signals are flagged as anomalous in the fault-free period, providing context for distinguishing routine deviations from potential failure evidence. Biased-Decision Correction identifies points where the model reaches different conclusions from the same initial analysis and uses preference optimization to favor more accurate diagnoses. Against baselines including the 14B OpsAgent and RCA-Agent with commercial models, our system with a 4B model achieves the highest or tied-highest accuracy on all four datasets, reaching 48.7% on Bank compared with 18.5% for OpsAgent.
items.title: Fault-Free Profiles and Decision-Level Training for Small-Model Root Cause Analysis

items.summary: We disprove a three-step error estimate for the Broyden--Fletcher--Goldfarb--Shanno {(BFGS)} method with exact line searches. We construct a globally strongly convex function $F\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ and a single nonterminating trajectory $x_k\to0$ for which $\limsup_{k\to\infty}\|x_{k+3}\|/(\|x_{k+2}\|\|x_k\|)=+\infty$. The Hessian of $F$ lies between $\tfrac12 I$ and $\tfrac32 I$ everywhere, and $F(x)-\tfrac12\|x\|^2$ is compactly supported with all derivatives vanishing at $0$. The proof first constructs point-gradient pairs satisfying the exact BFGS step identities. A five-step cycle produces a large three-step quotient and restores an invariant plane for the actual updated matrix, allowing the cycle to be repeated with arbitrarily small gradient errors. Disjoint smooth corrections to a quadratic then realize all the pairs by one objective. Strong convexity identifies the prescribed points with the unique exact line-search minimizers. Thus smoothness and strong convexity do not imply the proposed product estimate, even for an objective that agrees with a quadratic to every order at its minimizer.

items.summary: Support points provide a practical and effective way to approximate a probability distribution by a small set of equally weighted representatives through energy-distance minimization. In many applications, the variables satisfy convex constraints that the representatives should also respect. We investigate whether unconstrained support points automatically satisfy such constraints and show that this is not guaranteed. We construct counterexamples using three planar observations, a density with full triangular support, and positive-definite matrix data admitting an indefinite optimal representative under the Frobenius norm. We also identify cases in which containment holds, establish stability under distributional perturbations, and quantify the objective cost of imposing a convex-hull constraint. For a fixed number of representatives and a positive population constraint gap, empirical configurations with vanishing global objective error eventually leave the sample convex hull almost surely.

items.summary: State of the art latent dynamics world models achieve impressive performance for robot planning. But do they actually encode the physics of the world? In this paper, we show that popular world models today achieve strong results on tasks that reduce to image similarity but forget key details about objects in the scene like mass, deformation, friction, and bounciness. We achieve this by defining precisely what ought to be encoded in such a world model and introducing two new evaluation methods that can directly tease physical properties and easily scale to new ones. Our evaluation, which we call Roz, includes 10 contrastive tasks and 3 continuous tasks, totaling 1734 individual scenarios. We validate our eval on control tasks. On our own model, AnonWM, we find that performance roughly improves with training steps, while not necessarily being correlated with reconstruction MSE. We argue current model failures are a symptom of evaluation strategies (probes and planners) that are opaque, model-specific, and high-compute. Roz requires only a model that can ingest still frames or video, a way to extract latents, and a distance function between them, and it can be run in one pass. We hope future evaluations will adopt Roz's evaluation techniques. More broadly, we hope Roz can be a case study for a future where benchmarks allow rapid iteration and comparison across models.
items.title: Roz: A Taste Test for World Model Latents

We show that a brief surge can disrupt this reuse and trigger metastable failure in prefill--decode (PD) disaggregated engines: service remains degraded after arrivals return to a load the engine previously sustained. Slower calls prolong sessions and enlarge their aggregate context, or working set; the resulting cache misses increase recomputation and further delay departures. items.summary: Data flywheels promise continuous improvement via insights from deployment data. Understanding how the deployed model succeeds and fails can steer subsequent data collection towards patching failures and reinforcing successes. However, robot deployments create large volumes of high-dimensional rollout data, which is challenging to understand and confidently ground data collection decisions in. To make deployment data easier to analyze and act on, we propose behavior graphs, which compress policy rollouts into a single interpretable, directed graph. We construct the graphs by learning to identify similar behavior modes across rollouts, connecting the behaviors temporally, and finally linking them to outcomes. In a user study on three real-world tasks, where participants analyzed rollouts to choose a data collection strategy, 16 of 18 preferred behavior graphs to rollout videos, reaching comparable conclusions with 40.3% lower perceived temporal demand and 37.6% lower effort. Beyond interpretability for deployment data, behavior graphs are capable progress predictors: across 43 datasets, they improve the rank correlation between predicted progress and true temporal order by 22.9% and reduce mean absolute error by 53.5% relative to the strongest baseline. As the number of deployed robots grows, behavior graphs lend structure to high-dimensional policy rollouts and make deployment data easier to interpret and reason about.

items.summary: Action-conditioned world models are increasingly trained on data from randomized experiments, and whether their predictions respond to actions is usually checked by replacing or removing the actions and measuring the loss in accuracy. We show that such diagnostics report action effects where there are none: under autocorrelated designs, future actions stand in for history the model does not see, and a better model learns the stand-in better. When the design law is known, a conditional randomization test written as an e-value is valid in finite samples whatever the model, provided the resampler conditions on the full state the design used; resampling from a simpler law reproduces the false effect. We identify a second failure, specific to world models: when many sites share one action sequence (cells in a microscope field, pixels in a frame), the natural pooled score turns small model errors along the action contrast into overwhelming evidence against a true effect. In a pixel world, its median log e-value fell from $-17.3$ to $-6832$ as frames grew from 64 to 4096 pixels, while the oracle's rose. Tempering the score by a design effect estimated on training data changes the bet, not the validity. Our own preregistered analysis of optogenetic ERK experiments failed in exactly this way; a tempered statistic, selected on synthetic data and registered before the data were obtained, then rejected the null on a never-opened field ($E\approx 1.1\times10^{10}$). Every analysis is preregistered, fixed in a dated protocol before it was run, or labelled exploratory, and every reported result is generated from hashed result files.

items.summary: Anti-cancer drug treatment can induce tumor cells to adopt reversible drug-tolerant persister states, facilitating resistance evolution and eventual treatment failure. Although low-dose and intermittent therapies have been proposed as alternatives to maximum tolerated dose (MTD) therapy in this setting, it remains unclear when and why these strategies are optimal. To address this question, we develop a mathematical model of drug-induced persistence where the drug can promote switching to a drug-tolerant state or inhibit reversions to sensitivity in a dose-dependent manner. We uncover sharp transitions between qualitatively distinct therapy regimes, including intermittent high-dose and continuous low-dose therapy, driven by the relative dose sensitivities of cell death and phenotypic switching. In particular, intermittent treatment is optimal when the drug inhibits reversions at doses too low to effectively kill the sensitive cells. We finally exploit the simple regime structure of optimal therapies to show that robust alternatives to MTD therapy can be identified under incomplete knowledge of the underlying dynamics

items.summary: AI scientists are expanding automated research across scientific domains, yet their ability to turn the scientific record into a foundation for autonomous discovery remains elusive. Here we uncover a fundamental barrier to this transition and demonstrate a route to overcome it in computational quantum science, where advances shape both what we can learn from complex quantum systems and what quantum computing can ultimately deliver. To identify this barrier, we introduce OmniQ, an expert-audited virtual research environment that converts published studies into executable reproduction tasks. Across 59 papers spanning classical simulation, quantum algorithms and quantum-property characterization, we systematically evaluate five agentic systems powered by large language models and six third-party agent harnesses. Our findings reveal that current AI scientists often fail to reproduce published results, exposing a fundamental mismatch between what scientific papers communicate and what autonomous agents require. By contrast, human expert intervention can turn these failures into successful reproductions, showing that the missing information can be identified and converted into reusable research experience. Guided by this observation, we develop Residual Agents (RA), a quantum-tailored self-improving AI scientist that distils externally verified workflow repairs into such experience. RA substantially improves research performance under fixed base models and limited adaptation budgets. For example, RA raises DeepSeek V4.1 Flash performance from 68% to 85%, matching Claude Code with Opus 5 at a third of its cost despite using a weaker base model. We integrate all reproduced results into an extensible platform built on the model context protocol, making verified research workflows directly accessible to AI scientists and allowing new scientific papers to be continuously incorporated.
items.title: Reimagining computational quantum research with AI scientists

items.summary: A source-based quiz can help a computing teacher identify material to explain again, but its report must preserve the limits of the evidence behind that decision. We present ClassQuest, a prototype connecting teacher-reviewed question drafts, private student responses, topic reports and targeted retries. A Year 10 classroom account of an earlier prototype supplies 20 usefulness ratings from 24 invitees, with a mean of 8.0 and median of 9 on a ten-point scale. A Boolean-logic episode documents how immediate feedback, a teacher explanation and a fresh question were combined. We separate this account from a completed technical audit and reusable teaching guide. An exhaustive single-item audit found no count mismatches across 5,456 constructed response configurations, while diagnostic cases exposed a retry increase caused entirely by changing participation and a progression suggestion based on one learner's three answers. A further case shows that an unoffered retry can be labelled missing. A separate reporting companion distinguishes opportunity to respond, pending review and matched retry cohorts. Its completion-sensitivity check matched an independent oracle in 46,375 constructed states across roster sizes 1-30, identifying when unknown responses can change a reporting band. Our contributions are a source-linked formative workflow, executable examples of interpretation failures, and reporting and teaching materials for examining those failures. Neither the questionnaire nor the audit establishes improved learning; the findings identify reporting requirements and practical directions for formative teaching.

items.summary: Switching networks arise across physics, biology, and engineering, where interactions turn on and off due to communication limits, control protocols, failures, or scheduling. Most synchronization theory for switching networks of continuous-time oscillators relies on the fast-switching approximation, yet many systems operate outside this regime, where switching can produce unexpected and counterintuitive collective dynamics. We develop the first analytical framework for synchronization in non-fast-switching networks of saddle-focus continuous-time oscillators. Using Rössler and piecewise-smooth systems as canonical examples, we leverage a structural property of saddle-focus oscillators to reduce the variational dynamics to a linear system with constant coefficients, enabling a Floquet-theoretic stability characterization under periodic switching. The analysis identifies explicit switching intervals that stabilize synchronization even when neither switching mode nor the corresponding average system supports synchronization in isolation, thereby revealing the mechanism underlying the emergence of "windows of opportunity" at intermediate switching rates. We further derive a switching-dependent master stability function linking the network Laplacian spectrum to the switching rate. The master stability function provides two complementary routes to inducing or preserving synchronization: adjusting the switching schedule for a fixed network or adapting the network spectrum to a prescribed schedule through our constructive edge-pruning or edge-augmentation algorithms. These results provide a rigorous basis for understanding and leveraging intermediate-rate switching in the design and control of evolving networks.
items.title: Rate-selective synchronization in switching networks: when timing meets structure

items.summary: LLM agents show strong potential in software engineering tasks such as competitive programming and code synthesis. Existing benchmarks, however, largely focus on small-scale settings such as self-contained Python modules, leaving distributed systems, an essential class of production software, under-examined. items.summary: Large language models have demonstrated strong capabilities in structured reasoning and code generation, yet identifying an assembly fault does not guarantee the ability to generate executable rework programs. In interlocking assemblies, a locally plausible repair program may violate blocking dependencies, omit required recovery operations, or terminate in an incorrect configuration. We identify this challenge as fault-conditioned executable rework generation, where models must jointly reason about structural failures and generate programs that restore constrained assembly states. To benchmark this capability, we introduce FORGE-Bench, containing 4,000 tasks across 26 interlocking assemblies with five assemblies held out for evaluating generalization to unseen structures. We further propose FORGE (Fault-Oriented Rework Code Generation for Executable Interlocking Assembly), a structured state-to-program framework that decomposes rework generation into Rework Structuring and Action Grounding. Rework Structuring captures fault-induced recovery dependencies, while Action Grounding maps these dependencies into state-conditioned executable actions. Experiments show that locally reasonable repair code is insufficient for reliable assembly recovery, and that connecting structural recovery reasoning with executable action realization is essential for verified target restoration.

items.summary: Version 1.02, 3 November 2026. Acemoglu and Restrepo (2020) estimate that one additional industrial robot per thousand workers lowers a U.S. local labor market's employment-to-population ratio by 0.39 percentage points and its hourly wages by about 0.77 percent. Rebuilding their design from raw IPUMS, IFR, and EU KLEMS data, I reproduce these estimates bit-exactly. I then ask what conventional robustness checks leave open: which industries, places, periods, and shocks actually identify the estimate? The regression spans 722 commuting zones and 19 industries, but the variation behind an instrumental-variable estimate can be far narrower. The sign is robust; the support is narrow. Negative estimates persist across conventional specification changes, 60 strong European instrument windows, alternative U.S. treatment windows, and the published periods through 2014. Yet automotive carries about 84 percent of normalized absolute Rotemberg-weight mass, and automotive exposure in six Rust Belt states supplies 95 percent of the net first-stage covariance. Without automotive, the remaining 18 industry shocks do not strongly predict U.S. robot exposure. Longer horizons, later start years, and adding Germany to the instrument all strengthen it through the same margin. The automotive component shows no detectable relation to 1970–1990 employment and wage changes, and a direct effect of the instrument would have to absorb 72 percent of the reduced form before conventional significance disappears. Inference is weaker than the regional first stage suggests. With 19 underlying industry shocks, exposure-robust first-stage F-statistics are 6.2 and 6.3 rather than 34, small-sample Anderson–Rubin tests do not reject a zero effect ( p = 0.059, 0.063), and other implementations of the same test disagree; in known-truth simulations, nominal 95-percent state-clustered intervals cover in only 60–66 percent of replications. Measurement assumptions also bind. In the original penetration metric, perpetual-inventory robot capital preserves the estimates at 5 percent depreciation, but faster assumed depreciation counts the automotive installations behind the first stage as replacement rather than net additions, eliminating shock-level relevance at 10 percent and all relevance at 15 percent. The benchmark is reproducible and robust in sign, but it is identified from an automotive margin in historically industrial labor markets; that margin defines its scope and the concrete content of its exclusion restriction. More generally, coefficient robustness and breadth of identifying support are distinct properties that shift-share studies should report separately. items.summary: High-resolution video diffusion relies on attention over long token sequences, making attention efficiency critical to generation latency. Our analysis identifies repeated maximum reductions and accumulator rescaling in online softmax as a bottleneck in long-context TPU attention. We propose CLiS (Certified Loop-invariant Stabilization), a training-free, plug-and-play optimization for video diffusion inference. CLiS fixes per-row stabilizers before the KV loop and certifies numerical safety per head, falling back to online softmax when certification fails. It integrates into existing fused-attention kernels without changing model weights or architecture. On Wan 2.2 and LTX-2 across TPU v6e and TPU7x, CLiS reduces diffusion transformer (DiT) step latency by up to 19.6% relative to tuned online softmax without measurable quality loss. items.summary: Language models in customer-facing products must be continually updated, since the data they serve shifts over time. As retraining on the full accumulated data is impractical, each update should instead run on a small set of examples carrying the training signal of all data seen so far. The strongest current methods build this set by gradient matching, which synthesizes examples whose training gradients match those of the full data. However, they require ground-truth labels, run once on a fixed snapshot rather than on a growing stream, and are slow on large data. We introduce \textbf{OLGA}, which lifts these limitations. It distills unlabeled data by drawing the gradient matching targets from the model's own next-token predictions. Across five text classification benchmarks with phi-1.5, it improves accuracy by 10 percentage points over the strongest selection baseline using as few as five examples. OLGA also distills online data streams by keeping a running rehearsal memory of synthetic examples, which is re-distilled together with each new batch as it arrives. In the online setting, it outperforms the strongest selection-based continual baseline by 6.6 stream-AUC percentage points. Finally, our method scales to large data by pairing distillation with selection in a hybrid pipeline, letting selection handle the mild stage of compression and distillation the extreme one. It cuts runtime by 30\% versus distillation alone at similar accuracy, and beats the best selection-only pipeline by up to 12.6 percentage points.

items.summary: Learning-based approaches have increasingly been explored for SAT solving, with particular attention to improving branching decisions in conflict-driven clause learning (CDCL) solvers. These approaches derive branching guidance either from static structural properties of SAT formulas or from dynamic signals obtained through solver feedback and execution traces. However, these forms of supervision provide limited evidence about state-dependent branching effects, while different outcome measures may favor different branching choices. To address these limitations, we propose SAT-ACT, an outcome-derived learning framework for CDCL branching. We design three complementary outcome comparison criteria to extract action preferences from independent branching action rollouts initiated at the same solver state. The criteria identify preferences supported by the outcomes and leave comparisons unresolved when the evidence is insufficient or conflicting, instead of forcing an ordering using a predefined scalar metric. A state-conditioned network learns branching priorities from the extracted preferences and uses them to guide CDCL search directly without online action rollouts. We further introduce non-dominated heuristic action supervision, which retains the solver-selected action as a training target only when it remains non-dominated under these preferences. Solver-level experiments show that SAT-ACT consistently reduces CDCL search costs on three SAT families and improves PAR-2 on the SAT Competition benchmarks.

items.summary: We conducted 37 semi-structured expert interviews to examine how frontier AI evaluations reduce societal-level AI risks. Evaluations have become central to AI risk governance, despite their shortcomings being widely critiqued. Still, the case for how they reduce risks in practice remains largely implicit. Drawing on expert accounts, we reconstruct this case by identifying the mechanisms through which evaluations are expected to reduce risk, the assumptions underpinning those mechanisms, and the challenges those assumptions face. Our findings suggest that `evaluation-based governance' could contain foundational gaps which undermine risk-reduction strategies that depend on evaluations. Using thematic analysis, we identified three key pathways through which evaluations could reduce risk: by (i) making societal-level risks concrete to decision-makers and the public (raised in 18 out of 37 interviews), (ii) serving as a basis for governance commitments and regulation (18), and (iii) incentivizing a better risk culture within AI companies (16). However, these pathways often depended on shared assumptions that participants themselves doubted. The main challenges included, in order of frequency: (i) diminishing informativeness of evaluation results as model capabilities improve (21), (ii) measurement limitations that may be inherent to the evaluation paradigm (18), (iii) a lack of guarantees that evaluation results will be acted upon by companies or governments (16), and (iv) the degree of control and discretion AI companies retain over evaluation design, disclosure, and response (12). Participants also noted that evaluation-based governance could prove counterproductive, by functioning as a permission structure for developers' continued capability improvement (4). We finish by discussing the implications of our findings for evaluation-based governance, and what would improve its prospects.
items.title: The Promises and Limitations of Evaluation-Based AI Governance: Evidence from Expert Interviews

items.summary: Visual mental imagery (VMI) decoding uses brain activity to reconstruct internally generated visual scenes, providing a potential pathway for externalizing internal experiences and developing neuroprosthetic communication interfaces. However, progress is limited by the lack of dedicated, training-scale VMI datasets. Current VMI paradigms often rely on visual prompts or short-term memory images, introducing visual and mnemonic confounds that make it difficult to disentangle neural activity associated with endogenous image construction from signals driven by prior or concurrent visual input. Furthermore, existing VMI datasets offer limited descriptive control over individual visual attributes, making it difficult to systematically assess fine grained visual details. To address these gaps, we introduce AVID, the first dedicated training-scale 5.0 Tesla functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) resource for auditory-induced VMI decoding. AVID comprises approximately 67 hours of dense recordings from nine participants. The dataset is structured into two complementary splits: a scene-level complex split using naturalistic Mandarin descriptions and a controlled simple split with explicitly specified visual attributes. We further formalize a standardized evaluation protocol that decouples source-image consistency from semantic alignment, allowing for a more nuanced assessment of imagery reconstruction. Baseline qualitative and quantitative results show that current reconstruction pipelines remain limited on AVID, although the most successful reconstructions preserve recognizable scene level semantics from spoken descriptions. By combining dedicated training-scale neural recordings and standardized evaluation resources, AVID provides both a data foundation for imagery-specific model development and a benchmark for evaluating VMI decoding with substantially reduced sensory contamination.

items.summary: The self-controlled case series (SCCS) design is widely used in studies of rare events, for example of vaccine side effects. Conceptually, the design has two main features. First, it requires only data from individuals who have experienced the event of interest. Therefore, the design is especially useful when the outcome is rare and the available data come from surveillance or clinical records, say, of hospitalized patients. Second, because comparisons are made within single individuals, time-invariant confounding between treatment and outcome is eliminated. We formulate a set of sufficient identification assumptions for estimating the causal effect of vaccination on an adverse outcome under the SCCS design, drawing on ideas from the causal inference literature. Unlike the existing SCCS literature, we do not consider a parametric model as the starting point. This allows us to establish when and why the SCCS design allows identification of causal effects, using data from cases only. However, because the sufficient identifiability assumptions are implausible in some applications, we also develop statistical tests for the existence of a treatment effect that remain valid when only a subset of the identification assumptions holds.
items.title: Causal Inference from Self-controlled Case Series

items.summary: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization enables memory-efficient large language model (LLM) fine-tuning, and recent methods incorporate curvature-aware strategies. However, in the high-dimensional parameter space of LLMs, these methods inherently suffer from exploding gradient variance and prohibitive costs. Conversely, confining updates to a low-dimensional subspace reduces variance but discards critical high-dimensional information, degrading performance. This creates a fundamental dilemma: full-space optimization is informative but has high variance, while subspace optimization has low variance but loses information. To break this trade-off, we propose ENGINE (Endogenous Variational MultiScale). Inspired by computational mechanics, we adapt static Variational MultiScale (VMS) theory to dynamic optimization, treating low- and high-dimensional spaces as resolved coarse and unresolved fine scales. Through a multigrid-style V-cycle, ENGINE alternates between spaces, dynamically probing fine-grained information in the high-dimensional space and injecting it to correct the efficient low-dimensional sampling process. Under appropriate assumptions, statistical analysis characterizes variance reduction and correction of curvature-induced bias, and convergence analysis establishes a stationarity bound for the corrected coarse updates. Evaluations on standard LLM benchmarks show that ENGINE achieves higher accuracy and faster convergence than existing ZO methods, achieving up to a $2.61\times$ speed-up in forward passes with zero additional peak memory overhead. Code is available at https://github.com/AI4Science-WestlakeU/ENGINE.
items.title: ENGINE: Endogenous Variational MultiScale Optimization for Zeroth-Order LLM Fine-Tuning

items.summary: High-dimensional data from multiple sources often combine shared structure with source-specific variation. We study heterogeneous principal component analysis, which seeks to recover common and private principal subspaces when their dimensions are unknown. {We propose \emph{Feature Extraction (FE)}, a novel data-driven framework with two steps. First, the Eigenvector-based Spike-Count (ESC) estimator determines the number of principal components (PC) in each source using only sample eigenvector information, rather than eigenvalue-based criteria. Second, FE identifies the locations of common features by comparing bias-corrected inner products between sample eigenvectors across sources. These matches yield estimates of the common and source-specific subspaces without iterative optimization. We establish the consistency of our estimators under a spiked covariance model in a high-dimensional regime where the dimension and sample size grow proportionally. Simulations and applications to federated image data and U.S. housing prices demonstrate the performance of FE in rank recovery, subspace estimation, and data reconstruction.} Code is available at https://github.com/liwenbo-research/HeterogeneousPCA

items.summary: This paper studies bidirectional pedestrian flow on a cyclic network of corridors. Each corridor consists of two lanes, while pedestrians may enter or leave the network at junctions. The dynamics are based on a 1-D, bidirectional, two-lane Lighthill-Whitham-Richards-type model, in which lane changes are described through explicit, density-dependent transfer rates that favor motion toward the less congested lane. We propose a localized lane-guidance control input that biases lane-changing behavior without creating pedestrians or reversing their walking direction. Such guidance may represent, for example, recommendations provided by staff or information screens. Under meaningful assumptions on the external inflows, we prove the existence and uniqueness of an admissible uniform equilibrium. We then linearize the system around this equilibrium and study the placement of localized guidance zones through a spectral detectability condition. We prove that, for any prescribed decay rate, two guidance patches located in a single, suitably chosen corridor are sufficient to satisfy the spectral detectability condition for all critical adjoint eigenmodes. This condition is necessary for the exponential stabilizability of the linearized system. Numerical experiments illustrate the spectral properties of the model and study the robustness of the modal observability condition with respect to the geometry and distribution of the guidance patches.
items.title: Localized Lane Guidance for a Bidirectional Pedestrian Cyclic Corridor: Equilibria and Generic Actuator Placement

items.summary: Long-horizon tasks require large language model (LLM) agents to coordinate interdependent actions, a capability central to automating complex workflows. Stepwise group-based reinforcement learning provides finer credit than trajectory-level supervision, but reliable comparisons must account for differences in interaction history. Enforcing this consistency within the limited rollouts of each task can leave insufficient support for estimating action preferences. We propose Beyond-Local Policy Optimization (BLPO), which estimates task-progress advantages from experience shared across tasks and training updates. We summarize trajectory prefixes into task-progress states and abstract actions by their function, allowing corresponding decisions from different tasks to contribute to shared estimates. To control bias and noise from heterogeneous tasks, we accumulate context-relative returns in a global memory with balanced aggregation and reliability weighting. These global advantages complement local comparisons over normalized actions and trajectory-level credit without a learned critic or additional rollouts. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop with 1.5B and 7B policies show improved task success over the evaluated baselines under matched training budgets. Further analyses show faster learning and shorter trajectories with little computational overhead.
items.title: BLPO: Beyond-Local Policy Optimization for Long-Horizon LLM Agents

items.summary: The feasibility of updating and synchronising digital twins of actuated systems from operational data depends strongly on how the system is controlled and, consequently, on the data generated during operation. This establishes a direct link between control actuation and model identifiability. This work presents a reinforcement-twinning framework that exploits this link through three computational components. A Gaussian-process surrogate of the physical return combines the twin prediction, used as a calibrated trend, with a discrepancy learned from measured returns, allowing Bayesian policy search to exploit the twin without being tied to its predictions. Candidate policies are proposed around the policy that is optimal for the twin, while measured returns can expand this region. The resulting physical episodes are replayed on the twin after observer-based synchronisation with sparse measurements, and its parameters are identified by combining Bayesian optimisation with gradient-based refinement. Selected information-oriented episodes deploy an excitation policy to improve parameter identifiability. The framework is demonstrated on a Burgers-flow analogue of dynamic-induction control in wind farms, with a deliberately misspecified model structure. Despite substantially biased return predictions, the twin provides a useful starting policy and search region, placing the guided search ahead of unguided Bayesian optimisation from its first physical evaluations. This advantage is maintained when the search region is allowed to expand in response to changes in measured returns, whereas searches over-constrained by the twin-defined region are eventually overtaken by the unguided alternatives. The results support reinforcement twinning as a framework for jointly adapting models and control policies when physical interaction is limited and model discrepancy cannot be neglected.
items.title: Reinforcement Twinning via Twin-Calibrated Bayesian Policy Search and Replay-Driven Identification

items.summary: We derive the baryon, active-lepton, and dark-matter inventory of one scalar-completed electroweak event. The CCF covariant derivative creates the first-order wall and its chiral source; bounded-support Parisi–Wu (PW) and continuum transport are two resolutions of that source, while the weak anomaly converts the left-handed bias into baryon and lepton number. The fixed-root PW calculation gives η_B,1^PW = 5.26082 × 10⁻¹⁰; the matrix-resolved continuum reconstruction gives 5.13315 × 10⁻¹⁰. Their computed hard-scale response defines the non-Gaussian theory-resolution interval η_B = 5.26 (+0.30, −0.40) × 10⁻¹⁰, which contains the independent Paper II baryon-loading range (5.37–5.48) × 10⁻¹⁰. The same event produces the flavor-scalar active source L_ν = 4.022200 × 10⁻² (1, 1, 1) and ξ = 5.87649332 × 10⁻² (1, 1, 1). An equal right-handed counterasymmetry makes this a chiral separation rather than net lepton-number creation. On the Paper II background its direct weak-rate map gives Y_P^weak = 0.24527; counting the right and active radiation once gives Y_P^full = 0.24712. An exact reflection protects one odd closed-support scalar pole with J = 0 and M_X = 3.9230019 TeV + O(Λ_QCD). The allowed Φ_G^a B_i^a operator is a heavier transverse J = 1 excitation, not the ordinary static-source gluelump ground state. The Lorenz/support theorem gives the exact temporal-source identity J_(u,G) = 0, excluding a scalar-color Coulomb kernel and Sommerfeld ladder while retaining transverse color interactions. Deconfined freeze-out then yields Ω_X h² = 0.130 (+0.028, −0.015), overlapping the Paper II requirement 0.1230–0.1234 without a cosmological fit.
